Real-Time RAG Platform with Hybrid Retrieval

A self-initiated, end-to-end AI platform combining live web ingestion, hybrid retrieval, and a real-time WebSocket layer across three client apps.

Full-Stack & AI EngineerSelf-Initiated ProjectAug 2024 – Jan 2025

Overview

A personal project built to explore what a genuinely real-time, always-current RAG system looks like once you stop assuming a static knowledge base — spanning a shared backend, two frontend clients, and an admin dashboard.

Problem

Most RAG demos retrieve from a fixed, pre-indexed corpus that goes stale the moment the world changes. I wanted to know what it would take to keep a knowledge base continuously current from live web sources, and to make retrieval itself smarter than a single vector-similarity lookup.

Solution

I built LangGraph-based agentic workflows paired with live web-scraping NLP pipelines so the knowledge base updates continuously instead of going stale, and combined Qdrant semantic search with Neo4j graph reasoning so structured, relational queries aren't limited to vector-similarity alone. A real-time WebSocket layer with async processing keeps multiple clients in sync during a session, and all three clients — Next.js web, Flutter mobile, and an admin dashboard — share one API layer rather than duplicating logic per platform.

My role

I designed and built the full system end-to-end: the FastAPI backend, the hybrid retrieval layer, the LangGraph agent workflows, the WebSocket real-time layer, all three client applications, and the deployment pipeline.

Engineering challenges

Retrieval quality beyond vector similarity

Pure vector search struggles with structured, relational questions — 'what depends on what' isn't really a similarity problem. Pairing Qdrant with a Neo4j graph layer for relational reasoning is what pushed retrieval precision up by roughly 28% on that class of query specifically, without regressing plain semantic lookups.

Real-time state across concurrent sessions

Keeping multiple clients — web, mobile, and an admin view — in sync during a live session meant the WebSocket layer had to do more than push messages; it had to reconcile state across async workers. Building that on top of async processing is what cut end-user interaction latency by roughly 45%.

One API, three very different clients

Flutter, Next.js, and an internal dashboard have different rendering models and lifecycles. Rather than let each client grow its own copy of the business logic, I kept that logic entirely in the shared API layer, which is what cut duplicate frontend logic by roughly 60% and kept feature parity manageable across platforms.

Technical decisions

Hybrid retrieval instead of vector-only

Vector search alone is a strong default, but it isn't the right primitive for relational questions. Adding a graph layer rather than trying to force everything through embeddings kept each retrieval mode doing the job it's actually good at.

Async stack over a simpler sync one

500+ concurrent requests with sub-200ms median latency isn't realistic on a synchronous stack without heavy over-provisioning. Async PostgreSQL, Redis, and Celery let the system handle load spikes without the infrastructure cost of just throwing more sync workers at the problem.

Results

  • Reduced knowledge staleness by over 80% versus a static corpus, via continuous live-web ingestion.
  • 500+ concurrent requests handled at ~99.9% uptime with sub-200ms median API response time.
  • ~28% improvement in retrieval precision on structured relational queries versus vector-only baselines.
  • ~45% cut in end-user interaction latency from the async WebSocket layer.
  • ~60% reduction in duplicate frontend logic by sharing one API layer across three clients.
  • Cold-start deployment time cut from ~12 minutes to under 3 minutes.
